messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 56

The scrub sink hums the same low note it always has, but seventy-seven-year-old Dr. Kiet Nguyen no longer hears it as background noise. It pulls him back to Case 412. Thirty-two years ago, the operating room was colder. He stands at the far end of the table, his hands clean but his mentor’s gloved ones slick with blood. The monitor’s steady rhythm fractures into a flat, unyielding tone. He watches the junior resident’s shoulders drop, sees the chest cavity open, realizes too late that the clamp slipped. The patient’s chest rises one last time, then stills. The room holds its breath. Kiet does the same. He steps back. He files the chart. He goes home to his wife, Mai, and eats his dinner in the quiet dark. Now, decades later, the flatline lives in his bones. When Kiet closes his eyes, the fluorescent glare of that old OR replaces his bedroom ceiling. He wakes at 3:17 a.m. most nights, heart hammering against his ribs, mouth dry as paper. His hands shake as he reaches for the water glass. He doesn’t check the door locks again, not really; he just lies there until the shaking stops, listening to Mai’s even breathing, counting her exhales to anchor himself back to the room. He hasn’t slept through the night in eight years. He stopped attending rounds at the hospital last month. The thought of walking past Cardiovascular, of hearing the mechanical hiss of ventilators or the sudden cry of a code blue, makes his throat tighten. He tells himself it’s retirement. He tells Mai it’s time to spend more hours in the garden. But he spends those hours staring at the irrigation hose, watching the water arc through the air, convinced it will miss the soil and flood the pavement. He flinches when a car backfires down the street. He jumps when a neighbor’s dog barks at the mail carrier. The world has become too loud, too unpredictable, and his nervous system stays wound tight, waiting for the next alarm. At work, even before he stepped away, he avoided the trauma bay. When a colleague mentioned a recent MVA with multi-system injuries, Kiet’s stomach turned cold. He excused himself to the supply closet, gripping the metal shelves until his knuckles whitened. He couldn’t watch the younger surgeons struggle. He couldn’t bear the thought of standing beside them, helpless, while time slipped away. He remembers the weight of the sterile drape, the copper smell of blood, the quiet devastation on his mentor’s face. He tells himself he was just an observer. He wasn’t the one who held the scalpel. But observation is its own kind of witness. He sits across from me now, his posture rigid, his eyes tracking the dust motes in the afternoon light. He speaks in careful, measured sentences, as if controlling the pace of his words might prevent something else from breaking. He describes a dream where he is back in the gown, scrubbing his hands raw, but the water turns to sand, pouring through his fingers no matter how hard he tries to close them. He rubs his thumb over his wedding band, a repetitive, grounding gesture. Mai tries to hold him when the nights grow long, but he stiffens, afraid his tension will infect her. He pulls away, not from lack of love, but from the fear that his restlessness will pull her into the storm too. The garden is half-finished. The emails pile up on his desk. His body remembers what his mind has tried to seal away. He sits in the chair, breathing slowly, waiting for the next sound, the next shift in the air, bracing for a history that never asked him to carry it.
